blocks.text:
PERSONAL AND CONFIDENTIAL

Karen Lawrence
Chief Operating Officer
{{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}}

Re: Review of strategic alternatives

Dear Karen,

Thank you for the conversations you and the shareholders have had with us this spring, and for the candor with which they described what they want for the company and for themselves. This letter sets out the terms on which Quillon Harbor Advisors LLC will act as financial advisor to Ingram, Bowers and Roth in a review of its strategic alternatives, with our work commencing on {{fact:f:E-2023-001.start}}.
What the review will cover

The question the shareholders have put to us is simple to state and harder to answer: what should the owners do with the company over the next several years? Our work is to examine the {{fact:f:E-2023-001.scope}} we have discussed with them, running from continued ownership on the present footing through to a sale of the whole business, and to tell you for each what it is likely to be worth, what it would ask of the company and its people, and what could cause it to disappoint.

We will begin with the company as it stands, working through the historical financial statements with you and your finance staff and building the bridge from reported earnings to an adjusted figure that a buyer or a lender would recognize. From there we will value the business under its present ownership, set that value against what comparable companies trade for and what comparable businesses have sold for, and then measure each alternative against that standalone case, so that the shareholders are always comparing a choice with the course they would otherwise be on.

This is a review and not a sale process. We will not approach any prospective buyer, investor, or lender on the company's behalf without the shareholders' prior written approval, and where it helps to know how the market would receive a particular course, we will draw on our own conversations with acquirers and sponsors, describing the company by sector and size and never by name. Nothing in the review commits the shareholders to a transaction, and if they later decide to pursue one, that work would be the subject of a separate letter on its own terms.

I will lead the engagement myself and will answer for the recommendation we put in front of the shareholders. Jennifer Bruce, an Advisory Associate, will build the financial model and the bridge from management's figures to the adjusted ones; Sandra Norman, also an Advisory Associate, will run the information request and keep the record of what we have asked for, what has arrived, and what remains outstanding; and John Bauer, an Analyst, will prepare the comparable company and transaction analyses and our written status reports to you. We would like you to serve as our principal contact, and we will route every request for information through you so that your staff hear from us in one voice.

The schedule below sets out what you will receive from us and roughly when, counted from the commencement of the engagement. The later stages depend on how quickly information reaches us and on the shareholders' own calendar, and if either moves, we will tell you promptly how the schedule moves with it.

rows: Information request and kickoff session with management
Diagnostic of historical results, including the bridge from reported to adjusted earnings
Standalone financial model and valuation under present ownership
Comparable company and precedent transaction analyses
Assessment of each alternative: likely value, conditions, and principal risks
Heather Delacruz, Jennifer Bruce and John Bauer
Recommendation and presentation to the shareholders

blocks.text: Fees and payment

Our fee for the review is a fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2023-001.fee}}, and it does not depend on the course the shareholders choose or on whether they choose any course at all. We will invoice it in equal monthly installments over the term, together with reasonable out-of-pocket expenses at cost, and we will ask your approval before incurring any expense out of the ordinary; invoices are payable within thirty days of receipt.
Term and termination

The engagement runs for approximately six months from commencement, or until we have presented our recommendation to the shareholders. Either the company or Quillon Harbor may end it at any time by written notice to the other, in which case fees accrued and expenses incurred to the date of notice remain payable, and the sections of this letter on confidentiality and liability continue to apply.
Confidentiality

We will hold everything the company provides to us in confidence, use it only for this engagement, and share it only within our team and with the company's own advisors as you direct. Our written work is prepared for the shareholders and management of the company and may not be passed to anyone outside it without our consent, which we will not unreasonably withhold.
Limitation of liability

We will rely on the information the company provides without verifying it independently, and our work is not an audit, a legal opinion, or tax advice. The company agrees to indemnify Quillon Harbor and its personnel against claims arising out of this engagement, except to the extent a court finally determines that a loss resulted from our gross negligence or willful misconduct, and our aggregate liability to the company shall not exceed the fees paid to us under this letter.
Governing law

This letter is governed by the laws of the state in which our principal office is located, without regard to its conflict-of-laws rules, and it is the entire agreement between us on this engagement. It may be changed only in a writing signed on behalf of both the company and Quillon Harbor.

If these terms reflect your understanding, please sign where indicated below and return a copy to me. Once we have it, Sandra Norman will send you the information request, and we will settle a time for the kickoff session with your management team.
Yours sincerely,
The Decision at Stake: Which Path the Shareholders of Ingram, Bowers and Roth Take Next

To: Heather Delacruz, Jennifer Bruce, Sandra Norman
From: John Bauer
Re: {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}}, strategic alternatives review, kickoff

The engagement began on {{fact:f:E-2023-001.start}}. What the shareholders want from it is a recommendation they can act on, and everything we do between now and then should answer one of four questions. What does the company actually earn once owner compensation, related-party costs and one-time items are normalized? What is it worth under present ownership if management delivers its plan, and if it does not? How do the {{fact:f:E-2023-001.scope}} in the engagement letter compare with that standalone value, after tax and after what each would ask of the shareholders? And which one do we recommend, on what conditions?

items: Normalized earnings. Jennifer Bruce builds the bridge from reported to adjusted earnings, one item at a time, with each add-back tied to a source document. The likely items are owner compensation above a market salary, related-party costs, and anything management calls one-time. Sandra Norman runs the information request through Karen Lawrence and keeps the response tracker, so we work only from documents we have in hand. Anything we cannot document stays out of the adjusted figure until we can.

Standalone value. Jennifer Bruce and I build the standalone model on management's plan and on a lower case of our own. The lower case is not a forecast. It shows what the business is worth if growth runs at its own historical pace and not at the plan's. I prepare the comparable company set and the precedent transaction screen. We value the business on both cases, so the shareholders see a range and not a single point.

The alternatives. For each one we estimate the value to the shareholders, the conditions it depends on, and what it asks of them in time, control and continued involvement. The shareholders' agreement matters here, since its transfer provisions may rule some paths in or out, and Sandra Norman has it near the top of the request. Heather Delacruz sets the framing. I draft the comparison pages and Jennifer Bruce checks them against the model.
The recommendation. Heather Delacruz takes the analysis to a single recommended path, with the reasons the others rank lower. It goes to Karen Lawrence in draft before it goes to the shareholders.

blocks.text: Some things are out of scope, and it is worth saying so now. We do not contact buyers, investors or lenders about the company without the shareholders' written approval. When we need a view of how the market would receive a course, it comes from our own conversations, with the company described by sector and size only. We do not provide a quality-of-earnings report, tax advice or legal advice; where those questions come up, we note them for the company's accountants and counsel. We are not running a sale process. If the shareholders choose a transaction, that is a separate mandate under a separate letter.

A few working rules, so we are consistent from the start. Every request to the company goes through Karen Lawrence, and Sandra Norman logs it before it goes. Nothing leaves the office with the company's name on it unless it is going to Karen or the shareholders. I draft the monthly status report, and Heather Delacruz reads it before it is sent.
Next step: I will send Jennifer Bruce draft screening criteria for the comparable set, so we can agree them before the first data from the company arrives.
Working Session Minutes: {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}}, Strategic Alternatives Review

items: Karen Lawrence, Chief Operating Officer, Ingram, Bowers and Roth
Heather Delacruz, Managing Partner
Jennifer Bruce, Advisory Associate
Sandra Norman, Advisory Associate
John Bauer, Analyst

blocks.text: This was our first working session since the diagnostic of the historical results closed, and its purpose was to settle the earnings base on which every later piece of the review will stand. We took two topics, and these minutes record where each of them landed.

We began with the bridge from reported to adjusted earnings, which Jennifer Bruce walked through line by line, and most of the session's time went to the few items that turn on how the shareholders have chosen to pay themselves and to house the business. She was careful, as she always is, to keep the reported figures and the adjusted ones in separate columns of the discussion, so that each adjustment could be argued on its own merits and none of them disappeared into a total.

Karen Lawrence was comfortable with the treatment of owner compensation above a market salary, but asked that the related-party occupancy costs and the items management regards as one-time be held as provisional until the company's outside accountants have given their view. We agreed that the bridge would go forward on that basis, with the provisional items shown on their own lines so that no one mistakes them for settled figures.

The second topic was the information request, where Sandra Norman took us through what has arrived, what has been partly answered, and what is still outstanding, item by item and in the order of the original list. The monthly management accounts and the payroll summary are in and reconcile to the annual statements, the client contract files are partly answered, and the client-level revenue data has been promised by the finance staff but not yet sent.

The gap that matters most is the shareholders' agreement, since its transfer and buy-sell provisions bear directly on which of the alternatives are practical at all. Karen Lawrence undertook to obtain a copy from the company's counsel, and we agreed that the assessment of the alternatives should not begin in earnest until we have read it, while the client-level revenue data can follow behind it without holding anything up.

Out of the session, Jennifer Bruce will revise the bridge to carry the provisional items separately and hold it open for the accountants' view, which Karen Lawrence will seek alongside the shareholders' agreement. Sandra Norman will send Karen an updated response tracker so that both sides are working from the same list, and John Bauer will extend the comparable company set and begin the precedent transaction screen, which he expects to have in draft for our next session. I will set out the framework for comparing the alternatives in the next status report, and when we meet again the first item on the agenda will be the revised bridge.
Status Report, Late August to Mid-September: Strategic Alternatives Review for Ingram, Bowers and Roth

We are at the midpoint of the review and close to plan, with one item running about a week behind. The diagnostic of historical results is complete. The bridge from reported to adjusted earnings is final except for the related-party occupancy costs, where we still await the accountants' view. The standalone model is built on management's plan and on our lower case. Its valuation is the late item, because it depends on that last add-back. We also held two working sessions with management on the plan's assumptions, and those sessions shaped the lower case more than anything else this period.

We have narrowed the trading analysis to {{fact:f:E-2023-001.comparators}}, after removing businesses whose service mix or size made them a poor guide, and the precedent transaction screen is in draft. Every item on the information request is now in except the client-level revenue data, which Karen Lawrence expects from the finance staff shortly. We have begun measuring {{fact:f:E-2023-001.scope}} against the standalone case, starting with the information each one needs from the shareholders' agreement. Fees billed to date are within the fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2023-001.fee}} set in the engagement letter, and we do not expect that to change.

items: Related-party add-back. Owner: Jennifer Bruce. Trigger: the accountants decline to support treating the occupancy costs as an add-back. Adjusted earnings would fall, and so would every value built on them.

Consents under the shareholders' agreement. Owner: Heather Delacruz. Trigger: our reading of the transfer and buy-sell provisions shows that an alternative needs consents some shareholders may not give. That alternative would then carry a condition, or come off the list.

Client relationships held by the shareholders. Owner: John Bauer. Trigger: the client-level revenue data shows a large share of revenue resting on relationships the shareholders hold personally. Buyers would discount for it or ask for deferred consideration, and any sale path would need a transition plan for those relationships.

Financing conditions. Owner: Jennifer Bruce. Trigger: lenders tighten terms further for sponsor-backed acquisitions of businesses this size. A financial buyer would then pay less, and the gap between financial and strategic buyers would widen.
Information timing. Owner: Sandra Norman. Trigger: the client-level revenue data is still outstanding two weeks from now. The assessment of the alternatives would slip by the same amount.
Confidentiality. Owner: Heather Delacruz. Trigger: any sign that word of the review has reached employees or clients. We would agree a holding statement with you the same day.

blocks.text: Four things moved since the last report. The shareholders' agreement arrived, so the information risk is down to one item, the client-level revenue data, and Sandra Norman has it at the top of the tracker. The add-back risk is narrower than it was, because the accountants accepted the one-time items, but it is not closed while the occupancy costs are open.

We also retired one risk. The last report carried the credibility of management's plan as an open item. After the working sessions we are satisfied that the plan's early years track the company's recent results. The later years remain the main sensitivity, and the lower case is where we have put that doubt, so it no longer needs a line of its own.

Financing conditions is new to the list. We added it after our conversations with lenders this month, in which the company was described by sector and size only. Borrowing costs have stayed high, and lenders are asking for more equity in sponsor deals of this size than they did a year ago. That bears on the sale alternatives, not on the standalone case.

For the coming period, Jennifer Bruce finishes the standalone valuation once the occupancy question is answered, and I finish the precedent screen and the first pass at each alternative against the standalone case. Heather Delacruz reviews the framing of the alternatives before any of it comes to you, and Sandra Norman keeps the tracker current in the meantime.
Next step: we will take you through the draft standalone valuation at our next working session, and I will send you the pages two days before it.

blocks.text: We record the decisions first. The presentation to the shareholders will lead with a single recommended path, preparation for a sale of the company over the coming year, with continued independent ownership set beside it as the considered alternative and the remaining alternatives summarized with the reasons they rank lower. Values throughout will rest on the adjusted earnings the accountants have supported and will be shown as a range; no outside party will be approached until the shareholders have had the recommendation in hand and put their own questions to it; and the presentation will say plainly that a sale is the one course on which Quillon Harbor would expect to earn a further fee.

Karen Lawrence opened the discussion by asking whether a recommendation to prepare for a sale could unsettle employees before anything is decided, and we spent some time on how the presentation should treat timing so that preparation does not read as an announcement. We agreed that no one at the company beyond Karen Lawrence and the shareholders would see the presentation, and that how employees would be told, if the shareholders accept the recommendation, is a question for them and not for this document. Jennifer Bruce then took us through the valuation range on the adjusted basis, and John Bauer showed where the comparable companies and recent transactions place the company within it, which persuaded everyone that a single figure would claim more precision than the work supports.

Sandra Norman set out what a buyer's advisors would ask for that the company could not yet produce, chiefly the assignment terms in its client contracts and a clean record of the related-party arrangements, and that list is much of why the recommendation is framed around a year of preparation. I raised our own interest last, and we agreed that the shareholders should read it in our words before they have reason to wonder about it.

items: Jennifer Bruce: finalize the valuation pages on the adjusted basis and send them to Karen Lawrence for a factual check.
John Bauer: bring the comparable company and precedent transaction pages up to the latest available figures, with sources footnoted.
Sandra Norman: complete the readiness list of documents a buyer's advisors would request, marking which the company holds today and which it would need to prepare.
Karen Lawrence: confirm with the shareholders a time for the presentation and whether their counsel will attend.
Karen Lawrence and Heather Delacruz: prepare a short note for the shareholders on the employee question, to sit alongside the presentation and not inside it.
Heather Delacruz: draft the covering letter, including the statement of our interest in a sale, and review the full presentation before it leaves the office.
